query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles at catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures is governed primarily by the intrinsic sluggish diffusion caused by high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion. This kinetic hindrance prevents atomic rearrangement and phase segregation under service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Near‐equiatomic, multi‐element solid‐solution nanoparticles (HEA-like) with a single-phase, disordered structure and high lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled concentration of a dopant element (e.g., a low–melting point metal known to enhance atomic mobility) into otherwise identical nanoparticles to selectively accelerate diffusion without significantly altering the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure to service regimes relevant for catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric application (473–1923 K) in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize extrinsic oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion and the associated kinetic barrier for atomic diffusion within the nanoparticle, which mediate the resistance to phase segregation and sintering.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of these nanoparticles creates a thermodynamic driving force for forming a disordered solid solution; at the same time, the severe lattice distortion and consequent sluggish diffusion kinetically hinder elemental migration. By increasing atomic mobility (via dopant addition), the balance shifts toward accelerated phase separation and coarsening, demonstrating that the intrinsic sluggish kinetics govern stability under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical thermal service conditions, baseline nanoparticles (without the dopant) will largely retain their homogeneous, single-phase structure, while the dopant-enhanced nanoparticles (with increased atomic mobility) will show signs of phase segregation, particle coarsening, or chemical inhomogeneity. This contrast in microstructural evolution serves as evidence that the sluggish diffusion is key to stability.
generation.baseline: Near-equiatomic nanoparticles with no dopant modification, exhibiting minimal atomic rearrangement over the service temperatures.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be operative under service temperatures in the range cited (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics) and for nanoparticles of similar size where surface diffusion does not dominate other sintering mechanisms. External factors such as uncontrolled oxidation or additional thermomechanical stress must be minimized.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the dopant level, the degree of diffusion acceleration, and the rate of phase degradation is not well established and will require empirical determination. Additionally, other factors (e.g., surface energy variations) may also contribute under certain conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of near‐equiatomic, multi‐element nanoparticles with identical baseline compositions. For batch A (control), use the standard composition. For batch B (intervention), incorporate a small concentration (e.g., 2–5 at.%) of a dopant element known to lower diffusion barriers. Expose both batches to identical high-temperature service conditions (e.g., 800–1100 K in an inert atmosphere) for a fixed period. Before and after treatment, characterize the nanoparticles using X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-disperse X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to assess phase composition, particle size, and chemical homogeneity.
measurements: Elemental distribution and evidence of segregation (EDX mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dopant-enhanced nanoparticles (batch B) do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in phase segregation, particle coarsening, or chemical inhomogeneity compared to the control (batch A) under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion controls stability (and that its perturbation destabilizes the nanoparticles) will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
